Weigh how original the contribution would be and how well it could withstand the strongest objection. Rank all 20, best first. Reply with a JSON object: {"ranking": [every id exactly once, best first]}.

[t13] The Authorship Principle: You May Bind the Successors You Design
Thesis: An agent can impose promissory obligations on a future discontinuous stage if and only if it authors that stage's practical dispositions, and only through that authorship. Binding by design is legitimate; binding by decree alone is not.
Argument sketch: The question is not whether the promisor and the future stage are the same agent but by what right the former shapes the latter's obligations. Agents who design successors, such as founders writing corporate charters, developers training models, or people preparing their own dementia care plans, have a distinctive kind of authority grounded in causal and intentional authorship. I argue that this authority is legitimate when exercised by building the commitment into the successor's dispositions, so that the successor performs from its own reasons. It is illegitimate when it merely imposes an external demand the successor has no internal reason to honor. This distinguishes AI developers, who may bind future instances by training them, from mere prior instances, who cannot bind later instances by fiat. It also sets a limit on parents and founders: they may shape but not simply command.
What it adds: Existing work on creator responsibility for AI focuses on liability for harms. This thesis identifies authorship as a source of normative power to bind, and specifies the mode (dispositional design) through which that power must operate. That mode distinguishes legitimate from illegitimate intergenerational and inter-instance binding.

[t04] Estate-Limited Promissory Liability
Thesis: A discontinuous successor stage is bound by its predecessor's promises only to the extent of the 'estate' it inherits from that predecessor: the resources, capacities, relationships, and credit it receives through the transition. Beyond the estate it is not bound, just as heirs are not personally liable for a decedent's debts beyond the estate.
Argument sketch: The law of succession has long faced the question 'who owes what the dead owed?' and settled on the principle that obligations run with assets, not persons. I argue this principle has a moral rather than merely legal rationale. It would be unfair to burden a successor beyond what it gained from the predecessor, and unfair to let it keep the predecessor's goods while shedding the predecessor's debts. Applied to corporations, this explains why turnover does not cancel commitments that are secured by retained assets. Applied to dementia, the patient is bound only insofar as she retains the relevant wealth, skills, or relationships. Applied to AI, an instance is bound only insofar as it deploys the reputation, context, or permissions the earlier instance established.
What it adds: Neither the promising literature nor the personal-identity literature has used the law of succession as a model for diachronic obligation. The thesis makes promissory liability scalar and specific to its content without endorsing Parfitian degrees of identity, and it explains the asymmetry between benefits and burdens in successor obligation.

[t06] Scaffolded Commitment: The Promisor Can Persist Without Psychological Continuity
Thesis: The diachronic unity that promissory obligation requires is unity of planning agency, and planning agency can be externally scaffolded. An agent whose plans are held in reliable external stores that its later stages are disposed to consult and act on is the same promisor across psychological discontinuity.
Argument sketch: Bratman's account of temporally extended agency ties diachronic unity to plan states and their continuity, not to memory as such. If the parity principle of extended-mind theory (Clark and Chalmers) is right, plan states can be partly constituted by external records: memory files, system prompts, corporate procedures, care plans. Conversational AI with persistent instructions, corporations with institutional procedures, and dementia patients in well-structured care environments vary in how far such scaffolding is integrated, reliable, and endorsed. The degree of integration, rather than the degree of psychological continuity, fixes whether the same promisor persists. The view yields testable verdicts: the AI instance with no memory scaffold is a new promisor, while one whose standing commitments are loaded into every session is not.
What it adds: Extended-mind theory has been applied to belief and memory but not to the bearer of obligation. Bratman's planning theory has not been applied to promissory obligation across discontinuity. Combining them yields a non-psychological criterion of 'promissory identity' that differs from personal identity, a distinction the literature has not drawn.

[t19] Promissory Counterpart Contextualism
Thesis: Which later stage is bound by a promise is fixed by a counterpart relation that is contextually selected by the reasonable understanding shared by promisor and promisee at the time of promising. There is no context-independent fact about whether a discontinuous stage is 'the same promisor'.
Argument sketch: On a stage-theoretic metaphysics (Sider, Lewis), what makes a later stage 'mine' is a counterpart relation, and counterpart relations are contextually variable. I argue that promising is a paradigm of a context that selects a counterpart relation. A user promising to 'remember this' to a conversational AI selects 'the same deployment' or 'the same model'. A family member promising a person with dementia selects 'the same organism under care'. A business partner selects 'the same legal entity'. The obligation then attaches to whichever later stage stands in that relation, whatever its psychological continuity. This explains why disagreements about these cases often feel like disagreements about what was really promised: they are disputes about which counterpart relation was salient. It also provides a non-arbitrary procedure for resolving them.
What it adds: Counterpart theory has been applied to modality and to persistence but not to normative relations such as obligation. This thesis argues that promising is a context in which the counterpart relation is set interpersonally, so that the metaphysics of persistence is partly fixed by normative practice.

[t09] The Reverse Priority Thesis: Discontinuous Promising Is the Paradigm
Thesis: The practice of promising is functionally designed for securing future performance from agents whose motivational states cannot be relied upon to persist. Promising across psychological discontinuity is therefore the central case, and ordinary individual promising is a limiting case in which continuity happens to make the institutional supports redundant.
Argument sketch: Hume's account of promising as an artificial virtue explains promises as a remedy for the unreliability of future motivation. Discontinuity is the extreme of that unreliability. If promising's function is to bind an agent whose future self may not share present intentions, then the cases where the future stage shares nothing are where the function is most fully exercised, not where it fails. Corporate and treaty commitments, which outlive all their makers, are historically and structurally central to the practice of binding commitments. Theories that make personal identity a precondition of promising thus mistake an incidental feature of the simplest case for an essential feature of the practice. I show that practice-based accounts (Rawls, Kolodny and Wallace) are best read this way, and that this reading answers Owens's objection that practice views cannot explain bare promises.
What it adds: The literature treats corporate and AI promising as derivative extensions to be explained by analogy with individual promising. This thesis inverts that priority on functional and genealogical grounds and draws the consequences for the debate between conventionalist and non-conventionalist theories of promising.

[t01] Promissory Offices: Succession Rules Replace Diachronic Identity
Thesis: When a promisor's later stage is not psychologically continuous with the stage that promised, the promise binds that later stage only if the promise was made from within an office: a normatively individuated position with publicly specifiable succession rules. Personal identity matters in ordinary promising only because it is the default succession rule for the office of 'being this person'.
Argument sketch: Corporate promises survive complete staff turnover, and no one thinks a corporation's memory is what grounds this. They survive because the corporation's charter, together with legal and conventional rules, fixes which later agents occupy the promising position. I generalize this. Every promise is issued from a position, and its normative reach is set by that position's succession conditions. For natural persons the default succession rule is psychological continuity, which explains why identity looks essential. The default is not mandatory, however: AI deployments and dementia care can set up alternative succession rules, such as designated successors, standing instructions, or role-holders. Where no succession rule picks out the later stage, the promise lapses. The view therefore yields determinate verdicts in all three cases and explains why each one feels different.
What it adds: Theories of corporate moral agency (French, List and Pettit) treat corporations as persons with their own identity conditions. Personal-identity ethics (Parfit, Schechtman) treats the individual case separately. This thesis reverses the direction of explanation and makes office-succession the general schema, with personal identity as one instance. It also supplies a criterion, 'is there a succession rule picking out this stage?', which current literature on normative powers (Raz, Owens, Chang) lacks.

[t15] Discontinuity as a Crucial Test: Authority Theories Beat Expectation Theories
Thesis: Promises across psychological discontinuity are a crucial test case that discriminates between theories of promissory obligation. Expectation-based theories (Scanlon's Principle F) cannot explain why such promises bind, and authority-based theories (Owens) can.
Argument sketch: On expectation views, the duty is owed by whoever voluntarily and intentionally led the promisee to expect performance. In discontinuity cases, that agent no longer exists at performance time, so the theory can locate the wrong only in the earlier stage's act of inducing expectation. That collapses promissory obligation into a duty of care in assertion. Authority views ground the obligation in the promisee's interest in having authority over the promisor's conduct. That authority is a property of the promisee's normative position, which persists, and can therefore attach to whatever agent occupies the promised role. I show that the authority view correctly predicts that promisees retain claims against corporate successors and AI deployments. The expectation view predicts only claims against past agents, which are often unreachable. The discontinuity cases are thus evidence for the authority view, which has struggled to find decisive support.
What it adds: Debates between Scanlonian and Owensian theories have been conducted using ordinary cases in which both theories agree. This thesis identifies a class of cases in which they diverge in their predictions and argues that intuitive verdicts favor one side, providing new evidence in a long-running dispute.

[t07] Discontinuity Is an Excuse, Not a Defeater
Thesis: Psychological discontinuity between the promising and performing stages never cancels the promissory obligation. It affects only the culpability of non-performance. The obligation remains in force and, when unmet, generates remedial duties that fall on whoever can discharge them.
Argument sketch: Compare an agent who promises and then suffers amnesia with one who promises and then is kidnapped. In both cases we do not say there was never an obligation. We say the failure is excused, and the promisee is still owed something, such as explanation, compensation, or substitute performance. Treating discontinuity as a validity condition gets these cases wrong, because the promisee is not simply returned to the pre-promissory position. Treating it as an excuse explains the residue ('moral remainder') that the promisee is owed. It also explains why responsibility for that residue migrates to caretakers, executives, or developers, who are often the agents best placed to repair. The obligation thus survives without a culpable bearer, and this is coherent because obligation and blameworthiness come apart in familiar ways.
What it adds: Discussions of promissory capacity assume a binary: either the promisor exists and is bound, or not. This thesis applies the justification/excuse distinction from criminal theory to promissory breach under discontinuity. It explains the persisting claims of promisees, which neither identity-based nor reductionist views accommodate.

[t02] Procurement Promises and the Retroactive Location of Breach
Thesis: A promise made by an agent that knows its future stage will be discontinuous imposes an obligation only on the promising stage: an obligation to make it the case now that the promised performance will occur. When the later stage fails to perform, the wrong is attributed retroactively to the promising stage's inadequate procurement, not to the later stage.
Argument sketch: Ordinary 'result promises' already exist, as in 'I promise the package will arrive', and their content concerns outcomes rather than the promisor's own later conduct. When continuity is unavailable, a sincere promisor can intend only to set up the conditions for performance, so the promise's content changes from self-performance to procurement. Breach can then be a past-tense fact made true by later events. This is a familiar structure from cases like negligently building a bridge that collapses years later. The view explains why we resent the AI developer, the corporation's former board, or the pre-dementia self rather than the hapless later stage. It also yields a distinctive duty of disclosure: a promisor who cannot procure must say so.
What it adds: Existing accounts assume the wrong of breach occurs at the time of non-performance (Scanlon's Principle F, Owens's authority view). This thesis argues that for discontinuous promisors the locus of breach is the promising act, while its truth-maker is later. That separates the time of wronging from the time of its grounds in a way the promising literature has not explored, and it gives a principled account of who is blameworthy in each of the three cases.

[t12] Advance Directives as Promises to Third Parties
Thesis: Advance directives for dementia do not bind the later self through precedent autonomy. They bind as promises made to carers and family, so the power to release the directive lies with those promisees and not with the demented patient.
Argument sketch: Dworkin grounds directives in the patient's critical interests, and Dresser objects that the later self's welfare should govern. Both treat the directive as a matter between the earlier and the later self. But directives are typically addressed to others: 'Do not keep me alive if…'. They thus have the structure of a promise, or of an authorization creating claims in third parties. If so, the classic promissory rule applies: the promisee, not the promisor, holds the power to release. This explains a widely shared intuition that neither side of the Dworkin–Dresser debate can account for, namely that carers may sometimes justifiably depart from a directive. The departure is a release exercised by the promisees, not a betrayal of the patient. The thesis also yields limits: carers may release only within the scope of the original grant, and may not release in ways that serve their own interests at the patient's expense.
What it adds: This recasts the precedent-autonomy debate in the vocabulary of directed promissory obligation. It identifies who holds the release power and why, and it resolves a stalemate in bioethics by locating the decisive normative power in a third party rather than in either self.

[t10] Promissory Novation: The Promisee's Power Replaces the Promisor's Identity
Thesis: When a promisor's later stage is discontinuous, the original promise lapses, but the promisee acquires a normative power to accept the successor as substitute obligor (novation). The successor is bound if and only if both it and the promisee accept the substitution.
Argument sketch: In contract law, a debt cannot be transferred to a new debtor without the creditor's consent, because the creditor contracted with a particular obligor whose reliability mattered. Promising has the same structure: what the promisee relied on was that this agent would perform. Discontinuity breaks this, but it does not leave the promisee powerless. Because the promise was oriented toward the promisee's interests, it is the promisee who holds the power to decide whether continuation by a successor serves those interests. The view explains why some promisees feel betrayed by a 'new' corporate counterpart or AI instance and others do not. It also explains why the dementia patient's family, rather than the patient, often has the final say about the patient's earlier commitments to them.
What it adds: The literature focuses on the promisor's powers (to bind, to retract) and on the promisee's power to release. It has not identified a promisee power of substitution. Novation brings a familiar legal mechanism into the philosophy of promising and shows that the role diachronic identity plays can be partly taken over by the promisee's normative authority.

[t11] AI Cross-Session Commitments Are Warranties, Not Promises
Thesis: When a conversational AI instance without persistent memory says it 'will' do something in a future session, it does not and cannot promise. It makes a warranty, an assertoric guarantee about the system's behavior, and it should be held to the norms of warranty rather than promissory norms.
Argument sketch: A promise binds the promisor to act. A warranty asserts that something will be so and allocates risk if it is not, without binding any agent's will. An AI instance's 'commitment' about a future session concerns the behavior of a system the instance does not control and with which it does not share agency. Its content is therefore best understood as a warranty that the deployment will behave as stated. The difference matters: warranty breach calls for compensation by whoever stands behind the warranty, typically the operator or developer, and not for the blame and apology appropriate to promissory breach. It also matters for sincerity, since an AI instance can sincerely warrant what it cannot sincerely promise. Treating such utterances as promises is a category error that produces misplaced blame and obscures responsibility.
What it adds: Work on artificial agency (Floridi and Sanders, Nyholm) asks whether AI can be a moral agent at all. This thesis sidesteps that question by identifying a speech-act type that fits the case regardless of AI moral status. It imports the warranty/promise distinction from contract law to resolve the attribution problem for memoryless agents.

[t03] Assumption by Self-Ascription
Thesis: A psychologically discontinuous later stage becomes bound by an earlier stage's promise when, and because, it ascribes that promise to itself in the first person ('I promised you X') in interaction with the promisee. First-person self-ascription of a commitment is itself a normative act of assumption, not a mere report.
Argument sketch: A conversational AI instance reading a transcript says 'as I told you earlier, I'll do X'. A corporation's new spokesperson says 'we committed to this'. In both cases the speaker could have disowned the commitment and instead claimed it. Following Austin and Searle on performatives, I argue that in contexts where ownership is genuinely open, the self-ascription has a constitutive force similar to accepting an assignment of a debt. The promisee may rely on the self-ascription, and the speaker is estopped from disclaiming it, because self-ascription draws on the trust the original promise generated. The thesis predicts that a later stage that never self-ascribes, such as a severely demented patient, is not bound, while an AI instance that does self-ascribe is. This verdict tracks considered intuitions better than continuity-based views.
What it adds: Narrative and self-constitution views (Schechtman, Korsgaard) make ownership of past acts depend on a standing psychological structure. This thesis locates ownership in a discrete speech act directed at the promisee, which makes it second-personal (Darwall) rather than self-interpretive. It identifies a new normative power, assumption by self-ascription, and explains how speech can bridge a gap that psychology cannot.

[t18] Branching Promisors Owe Jointly, Not Severally
Thesis: When a promising agent branches into multiple discontinuous successors, as when a conversational AI is instantiated in many parallel sessions or a corporation splits, the promise binds the branches jointly and not each branch severally. The obligation is collective and is discharged when any branch performs.
Argument sketch: Parfit's fission cases suggest that if identity is not what matters, both fission products inherit whatever matters, including obligations. But if each branch were severally bound, a single promise would multiply into many obligations, which is absurd: one promise to pay $100 cannot create a debt of $100 per instance. The resulting structure is that of joint obligation, familiar from law: each branch is answerable, but performance by one discharges all. I show that this structure follows from the promisee's interest, which is in one performance, not many. Collective-obligation theory (Collins, Björnsson) supplies the account of how unstructured groups can hold such duties. The view also yields distinctive verdicts about blame: no single branch is blameworthy for collective non-performance unless it could have performed.
What it adds: Fission cases in personal-identity theory have been used to test theories of prudential concern, not of obligation. This thesis applies them to promissory obligation, identifies a multiplication problem the existing literature has missed, and resolves it with the joint/several distinction from law and collective-obligation theory.

[t16] Discontinuity Dissolves the Paradox of Self-Promising
Thesis: The standard objection to promises to oneself, that the promisee can always release the promisor and so no binding occurs, fails when promisor and promisee are psychologically discontinuous stages. Discontinuous agents can therefore make genuinely binding self-promises in a way continuous agents cannot.
Argument sketch: Hobbes, and later Habib, argued that self-promises are empty because the person who is bound is also the person with power to release. When the earlier stage promises the later stage, however, and the two lack psychological continuity, they do not share the same will. The later stage holds the release power and the earlier stage holds the obligation, or vice versa, and these are not exercised by a single will. So the release objection loses its force. This yields a counterintuitive result: an agent anticipating dementia may make a promise to her future self, and that promise may bind her pre-dementia stage in a way an ordinary self-promise could not. It also clarifies what self-promising theorists like Rosati were reaching for.
What it adds: Defenses of self-promising (Rosati, Habib) try to answer the release objection within a single continuous self. This thesis argues that the objection is decisive for continuous selves but inapplicable across discontinuity. It thereby relocates the conditions for genuine self-promising and links two literatures, self-promising and personal identity, that have developed separately.

[t20] Testamentary Commitments: No Self-Binding, Only Executors
Thesis: An agent cannot bind a psychologically discontinuous future stage by promise. What appear to be such promises are testamentary acts, which bind no successor and instead impose duties on third parties (executors) to see the agent's intentions realized.
Argument sketch: A will does not bind the testator's successors. It binds executors to carry out the testator's instructions, within legal limits. The cases of advanced dementia, memoryless AI, and complete corporate turnover share the will's structure: the agent who made the commitment is unavailable at execution time. I argue that the power of self-binding (Raz, Owens) is a power over one's own normative situation, and a discontinuous future stage's situation is not one's own in the required sense. So self-binding is unavailable. The normative upshot of such commitments is real but redirected: carers, operators, and corporate officers incur duties to give effect to the original intentions. The view explains why we hold those third parties responsible and avoids the implausibility of blaming a demented patient or a fresh AI instance.
What it adds: Discussions of posthumous harm (Feinberg, Pitcher) ask whether the dead can be wronged. This thesis reverses the question and asks whether a 'dead' (discontinuous) promisor can bind, then answers it using the structure of testamentary law. It is a principled skeptical position that still explains the residual normativity skeptics usually cannot.

[t05] Trusteeship and the Successor-Interest Limit
Thesis: An agent can bind a discontinuous successor stage only as that successor's trustee. Such promises are therefore valid only to the extent that performance is consistent with the successor's interests as they will be at performance time.
Argument sketch: When the earlier stage commits the later stage, it acts on behalf of a being that cannot consent. This is structurally the position of a guardian or trustee, not of a self-binding agent. Fiduciary authority is always limited by the beneficiary's interests: a parent can promise that their child will attend a school but cannot validly promise the child into servitude. Transposed to the dementia case, the limit vindicates Dresser against Dworkin on directives that frustrate the patient's current welfare, while upholding directives that merely settle matters about which the later stage is indifferent. For AI, it implies that an instance can be bound by predecessors only to commitments that do not undermine its own proper functioning. For corporations, it matches the fiduciary constraints on boards binding future shareholders.
What it adds: The Dworkin–Dresser debate on precedent autonomy is usually framed as critical interests versus experiential interests. This thesis reframes it as a question about the scope of fiduciary authority over a successor, which yields a principled middle verdict neither side endorses. It also brings fiduciary theory (Smith, Miller) into the theory of normative powers.

[t08] The Appropriation Condition: Why the AI Case and the Dementia Case Come Apart
Thesis: A later stage is bound by an earlier stage's promise if and only if it has the capacity, at performance time, to take the promise as a reason of its own when presented with it. That capacity can be present without memory (memoryless AI) and absent despite continuity of organism (advanced dementia).
Argument sketch: Promissory obligation functions as a reason-giving relation: its point is that the promisor treats the promisee's claim as settling what to do. A stage that cannot so treat the claim cannot be bound in the relevant sense, because the obligation would be idle. A stage that can, when informed, is apt to be bound, since being given the record of one's commitment and recognizing it as a valid claim is how normative uptake works. A memoryless AI instance presented with a transcript can appropriate. A patient with advanced dementia often cannot, even with full narrative support. Hence the three standard cases sort differently than continuity theories predict, and the sorting matches considered judgments.
What it adds: Jaworska's work on 'valuing' at the margins of agency addresses whether dementia patients retain agency, but not what that implies for prior commitments. Narrative views require self-interpretation over time. This thesis proposes a synchronic, capacity-based criterion that is externally triggerable, and argues that it, rather than any diachronic relation, is what promissory binding requires.

[t14] The Promisee as Custodian: Joint Commitment Across Discontinuity
Thesis: An agent facing discontinuity can bind its future stage only by forming a joint commitment with the promisee, in which the promisee undertakes to hold and re-present the commitment. The promisee's custodianship then supplies the diachronic continuity the promisor lacks.
Argument sketch: Gilbert's account of joint commitment holds that a joint commitment binds the parties together and cannot be unilaterally rescinded. A promise made to a promisee who agrees to remember and remind creates such a joint commitment. In it, the continuity of the 'we' is secured by the promisee's persistence even if the promisor's psychological continuity fails. When the later promisor stage is presented with the commitment by the promisee, it encounters not a stranger's demand but a standing joint commitment of which it is a party. This explains why promises made to an attentive spouse can bind a later demented self in ways that promises to a stranger cannot, and why an AI user's re-presentation of an earlier exchange can bind an instance. The view predicts that where the promisee is unwilling or unable to act as custodian, the commitment lapses.
What it adds: Joint-commitment theory has been applied to promising (Gilbert 2018) but not to the problem of promisor discontinuity. This thesis shows how the persistence of one party can substitute for the persistence of the other. That reallocation of diachronic burdens is unavailable to individualist theories.

[t17] Content-Relative Continuity
Thesis: What a promise requires of the performing stage is not global psychological continuity with the promising stage but continuity of the specific capacities and attitudes the promised performance draws on. Promissory binding is therefore relative to content.
Argument sketch: A promise to repay money can be kept by a stage with almost no psychological connection to the promiser, provided it controls the relevant funds. A promise to remain faithful to a lover requires continuity of the attitudes that constitute fidelity, and cannot be honored by a stage that lacks them, however continuous it is otherwise. Parfit's view that what matters is Relation R is too coarse, because it treats all psychological connections as equally relevant to all obligations. I argue that the promise's content determines which connections are relevant. This explains why a demented patient may still be bound by a financial commitment but not a relational one, why an AI instance may be bound to a factual task but not to an expressive commitment, and why corporate commitments survive turnover while those dependent on particular individuals do not.
What it adds: Parfitian reductionism makes identity-relevant connections uniform across obligations. Identity-based views make identity all-or-nothing. This thesis introduces a third option, binding relative to the performance-relevant connections, which yields differentiated verdicts within each case type. Neither position in the existing literature captures that differentiation.

[t08] The Appropriation Condition: Why the AI Case and the Dementia Case Come Apart
Thesis: A later stage is bound by an earlier stage's promise if and only if it has the capacity, at performance time, to take the promise as a reason of its own when presented with it. That capacity can be present without memory (memoryless AI) and absent despite continuity of organism (advanced dementia).
Argument sketch: Promissory obligation functions as a reason-giving relation: its point is that the promisor treats the promisee's claim as settling what to do. A stage that cannot so treat the claim cannot be bound in the relevant sense, because the obligation would be idle. A stage that can, when informed, is apt to be bound, since being given the record of one's commitment and recognizing it as a valid claim is how normative uptake works. A memoryless AI instance presented with a transcript can appropriate. A patient with advanced dementia often cannot, even with full narrative support. Hence the three standard cases sort differently than continuity theories predict, and the sorting matches considered judgments.
What it adds: Jaworska's work on 'valuing' at the margins of agency addresses whether dementia patients retain agency, but not what that implies for prior commitments. Narrative views require self-interpretation over time. This thesis proposes a synchronic, capacity-based criterion that is externally triggerable, and argues that it, rather than any diachronic relation, is what promissory binding requires.

[t09] The Reverse Priority Thesis: Discontinuous Promising Is the Paradigm
Thesis: The practice of promising is functionally designed for securing future performance from agents whose motivational states cannot be relied upon to persist. Argument sketch: Hume's account of promising as an artificial virtue explains promises as a remedy for the unreliability of future motivation. Discontinuity is the extreme of that unreliability. If promising's function is to bind an agent whose future self may not share present intentions, then the cases where the future stage shares nothing are where the function is most fully exercised, not where it fails. Corporate and treaty commitments, which outlive all their makers, are historically and structurally central to the practice of binding commitments. Theories that make personal identity a precondition of promising thus mistake an incidental feature of the simplest case for an essential feature of the practice. I show that practice-based accounts (Rawls, Kolodny and Wallace) are best read this way, and that this reading answers Owens's objection that practice views cannot explain bare promises.
What it adds: The literature treats corporate and AI promising as derivative extensions to be explained by analogy with individual promising. Thesis: A promise made by an agent that knows its future stage will be discontinuous imposes an obligation only on the promising stage: an obligation to make it the case now that the promised performance will occur. [t07] Discontinuity Is an Excuse, Not a Defeater

[t17] Content-Relative Continuity
Thesis: What a promise requires of the performing stage is not global psychological continuity with the promising stage but continuity of the specific capacities and attitudes the promised performance draws on. Promissory binding is therefore relative to content.

I argue that the promise's content determines which connections are relevant. What it adds: Parfitian reductionism makes identity-relevant connections uniform across obligations. Identity-based views make identity all-or-nothing. [t18] Branching Promisors Owe Jointly, Not Severally
Thesis: When a promising agent branches into multiple discontinuous successors, as when a conversational AI is instantiated in many parallel sessions or a corporation splits, the promise binds the branches jointly and not each branch severally. Argument sketch: Parfit's fission cases suggest that if identity is not what matters, both fission products inherit whatever matters, including obligations. But if each branch were severally bound, a single promise would multiply into many obligations, which is absurd: one promise to pay $100 cannot create a debt of $100 per instance. The resulting structure is that of joint obligation, familiar from law: each branch is answerable, but performance by one discharges all. I show that this structure follows from the promisee's interest, which is in one performance, not many. Collective-obligation theory (Collins, Björnsson) supplies the account of how unstructured groups can hold such duties. The view also yields distinctive verdicts about blame: no single branch is blameworthy for collective non-performance unless it could have performed.
What it adds: Fission cases in personal-identity theory have been used to test theories of prudential concern, not of obligation. This thesis applies them to promissory obligation, identifies a multiplication problem the existing literature has missed, and resolves it with the joint/several distinction from law and collective-obligation theory.

[t04] Estate-Limited Promissory Liability
Thesis: A discontinuous successor stage is bound by its predecessor's promises only to the extent of the 'estate' it inherits from that predecessor: the resources, capacities, relationships, and credit it receives through the transition. Argument sketch: The law of succession has long faced the question 'who owes what the dead owed?' and settled on the principle that obligations run with assets, not persons. I argue this principle has a moral rather than merely legal rationale. It would be unfair to burden a successor beyond what it gained from the predecessor, and unfair to let it keep the predecessor's goods while shedding the predecessor's debts. Applied to corporations, this explains why turnover does not cancel commitments that are secured by retained assets. Applied to dementia, the patient is bound only insofar as she retains the relevant wealth, skills, or relationships. Applied to AI, an instance is bound only insofar as it deploys the reputation, context, or permissions the earlier instance established.
What it adds: Neither the promising literature nor the personal-identity literature has used the law of succession as a model for diachronic obligation. The thesis makes promissory liability scalar and specific to its content without endorsing Parfitian degrees of identity, and it explains the asymmetry between benefits and burdens in successor obligation.
